analysis.one_liner: Bars Medicare-participating hospitals and clinics from forcing nurses to work beyond scheduled shifts or 12-hour stretches.
analysis.headline: Despite a bipartisan introduction and six cosponsors, the bill never received a hearing, markup, or vote; it died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have made Medicare participation conditional on limiting mandatory nurse overtime: hospitals, surgical centers, home health agencies, and clinics could not force a nurse to work past a scheduled shift, more than 48 hours a week, or more than 12 hours in a row, and nurses would get a 10-hour break after a 12-hour shift. On-call time would count as work. Nurses who refused illegal overtime or reported violations would be protected from retaliation, and violators could face civil fines up to $10,000 per knowing violation. True disasters would get an exception, but chronic understaffing would not count as an emergency.
analysis.who_benefits: Registered nurses and licensed practical nurses at Medicare-participating hospitals, surgical centers, home health agencies, and clinics would gain enforceable limits on forced overtime — a hard stop at their scheduled shift, 48 hours a week, 12 consecutive hours, and a 10-hour break after a 12-hour shift — plus on-call time counted as work, protection from retaliation, and a complaint process with real penalties for violators. Patients would be cared for by better-rested nurses; the bill's findings cite research linking long hours to fatigue, impaired vigilance, and medical errors, and note that more than 13 percent of newly licensed nurses hold second paid jobs [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Caps mandatory overtime for nurses: no required work beyond a scheduled shift, 48 hours a week, or 12 consecutive hours, plus a required 10-hour break after the 12th hour worked.
Counts required meetings, training, and on-call or standby time as hours worked, closing a common workaround.

Protects nurses who refuse illegal overtime or report violations from firing, discipline, or retaliation — including being reported to state licensing boards — and creates a complaint process the Secretary must investigate, with corrective action plans for violators.
Attaches enforcement: civil money penalties up to $10,000 per knowing violation, steeper penalties for repeat violators, and public listing of penalized providers on the HHS website.

Requires providers to post nurses' rights, keep written overtime policies available to staff, and post nurse schedules, and directs federal studies of safe maximum nursing hours, including at VA and Defense Department facilities.

analysis.who_pays: Hospitals and other covered Medicare providers would lose the ability to fill short-notice staffing gaps by compelling extra shifts, and would carry new duties: written overtime policies, posted rights notices, published schedules, and exposure to civil money penalties up to $10,000 per knowing violation, with violators publicly named on the HHS website [S3]. They would have to cover unpredictable demand through hiring or voluntary overtime instead [S3].

drawbacks.text: The bill's own findings concede 'potential pitfalls of discontinuity in care': forcing a handoff at 12 hours can itself introduce error risk, and some clinicians argue continuity sometimes outweighs fatigue.

Because the emergency exception explicitly excludes 'consistent understaffing,' a facility that is always short-handed would have no way to compel coverage no matter how severe the gap — leaving it to hire agency staff at higher cost, close beds, or cancel services.

Providers would bear real compliance costs: written overtime policies, posted rights notices, published schedules, and exposure to civil money penalties of up to $10,000 per knowing violation, with violators publicly named on a federal website.

Counting on-call and standby time as hours worked — even when the nurse is not required to be on site — would force home health agencies and clinics to rework how they staff overnight and weekend coverage.

The bill caps only compulsory hours. A nurse who volunteers for back-to-back or extra shifts faces no limit, so total hours worked — and the fatigue that comes with them — would not be fully addressed.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The safety case is supported by the bill's own findings: long shifts are linked to fatigue, impaired vigilance, and medical errors, and 18 states have already imposed similar restrictions, so a federal floor would extend a practice more than a third of the country has accepted [S3]. The design is careful — voluntary overtime is untouched, true disasters get a conditioned exception, stronger state laws and union agreements stand, and enforcement runs through a complaint process rather than blanket audits [S3]. The honest costs are real but modest: providers lose a scheduling tool, take on documentation and posting duties, and face penalty exposure, and facilities with chronic understaffing get no relief valve — they would have to fix the shortage by hiring or curtail services [S3]. The deepest fatigue risk is only partly addressed, since a nurse who volunteers for consecutive shifts faces no cap [S3].

outcome.mechanism: It sat in two House committees without ever getting a hearing or a vote until the 118th Congress expired in January 2025, and bills that don't pass before a Congress ends die and must start over.

narrative.text: Rep. Doris Matsui introduced the bill on March 5, 2024, with Rep. Jen Kiggans as the other original sponsor; the House referred it to both the Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means Committees the same day.
The bill was referred to the Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee on March 8, 2024, and referred again to that subcommittee on December 17, 2024.
No hearing, markup, or floor vote ever appears in the action record — those two subcommittee referrals were the last action the bill received.
Support stayed small: six cosponsors in total, one Republican and five Democrats.
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, so the bill expired and any future attempt would need to be reintroduced from scratch in the new Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hospitals, home health agencies, and other Medicare providers keep their current ability to require overtime to cover staffing gaps, with no new penalties or paperwork; nurses and patients gained no new federal protection.

for.name: Rep. Doris Matsui
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, with findings citing research that long nurse hours contribute to fatigue, impaired vigilance, and medical errors, and noting 18 states already restrict mandatory overtime.

for.name: Rep. Jen Kiggans
for.role: U.S. Representative (VA-02); original cosponsor and the bill's only Republican cosponsor
for.what_they_did: Joined Matsui in introducing the bill, giving it bipartisan sponsorship from day one.

for.name: Five House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Added their names, bringing total support to six members — one Republican and five Democrats.

against.name: Cathy McMorris Rodgers
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: The bill's primary committee never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill sat in its Health Subcommittee from March 2024 until the Congress ended.

against.name: Jason Smith
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: The second committee of referral took no action on the bill at any point during the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was introduced on a bipartisan basis — a Democratic sponsor and one Republican among six cosponsors — but it never reached a vote in the Republican-controlled House, so no one's position was ever tested on the record.

industries.industry: Hospitals (general, psychiatric, critical access, and hospital outpatient departments)
industries.note: They would lose the ability to compel nurses past scheduled shifts or 12-hour limits to cover gaps, and would face documentation, notice, and schedule-posting duties with fines up to $10,000 per knowing violation. Because the bill died, their current flexibility and cost control are untouched.

On-call and standby time would count as hours worked even when the nurse is not required to be on site, directly constraining how these agencies staff overnight and weekend coverage. The bill's death preserves the status quo.

industries.industry: Other Medicare providers (ambulatory surgical centers, rehab agencies, rural health clinics, federally qualified health centers)
industries.note: The same Medicare participation condition and penalty exposure would apply to them, limiting forced overtime as a staffing tool. They keep current flexibility because the bill never advanced.
